sentences: Besides, Rodolphe added, perhaps, from the world's perspective, one is right?
Well then!
he said, don't you know that there are souls that are constantly tormented?
They need both dreams and action, the purest passions, the most intense pleasures, and thus one throws oneself into all sorts of fantasies and madness.
Then she looked at him as one gazes at a traveler who has passed through extraordinary lands, and she continued: "And that is what you have understood, the Counselor said.
You, farmers and workers of the countryside; you, peaceful pioneers of a work entirely of civilization!
you, men of progress and morality!
you have understood, I say, that political storms are indeed more fearsome than the disorders of the atmosphere..."
One day, he said again, all of a sudden, when one had almost given up hope.
Then horizons begin to open up; it's like a voice shouting, 'There he is!' You feel the need to confide your life to this person; to give them everything, to sacrifice everything for them!
You can't explain it; you just sense it.
You've glimpsed each other in your dreams.
(And he was looking at her.) Finally, there it is, the treasure you've searched for so long, right in front of you; it shines, it sparkles.
Yet you still have doubts; you don't dare to believe it; you're left dazzled, as if emerging from darkness into light.
And as he finished these words, Rodolphe added a gesture to his phrase.
He ran his hand over his face, like a man who is dizzy; then he let it fall onto Emma's.
She withdrew hers.
But the Counselor was still reading: 'And who would be surprised by this, gentlemen?
Only someone who would be blind enough, deeply immersed (I don't hesitate to say), deeply immersed in the prejudices of another age to still misunderstand the spirit of the agricultural populations.
Where, indeed, can one find more patriotism than in the countryside, more dedication to the public cause, more intelligence in a word?

And I don't mean, gentlemen, this superficial intelligence, a vain ornament of idle minds, but rather this deep and moderate intelligence, which above all else seeks to pursue useful goals, thereby contributing to the good of each individual, to the common improvement, and to the support of the states, the fruit of respect for the laws and the practice of duties...'

sentences: His intention was to settle in this last city, which he had been assured was a city of pleasures.

He had barely traveled three leagues into the Roman countryside when night began to fall; Danglars had not thought he would leave so late, otherwise he would have stayed; he asked the postilion how far it was to the next town.
Danglars still felt a remnant of the well-being he had experienced the day before, which had given him such a good night's sleep.
He was comfortably stretched out in a good English coach with double springs; he felt himself being carried along by the gallop of two fine horses; he knew the relay was seven leagues long.
What to do when you are a banker and have happily gone bankrupt?

Danglars thought for ten minutes about his wife who remained in Paris, another ten minutes about his daughter traveling the world with Mlle d'Armilly, he spent another ten minutes on his creditors and how he would use their money; then, having nothing left to think about, he closed his eyes and fell asleep.
Danglars continued to sleep, telling himself that he would have plenty of time to wake up at the relay.
The carriage stopped; Danglars thought he was finally reaching the long-desired destination.

He opened his eyes, looked through the window, expecting to find himself in the middle of some city, or at least some village; but he saw nothing but a kind of isolated hovel, and three or four men moving about like shadows.

Danglars waited a moment for the postilion who had finished his relay to come and ask him for the fare; he planned to take the opportunity to ask his new driver for some information, but the horses were unhitched and replaced without anyone coming to ask the traveler for money.
Danglars, surprised, opened the door; but a strong hand immediately pushed it back, and the carriage rolled on.
It was still some romantic Italian that Danglars had remembered when his daughter sang duets with Prince Cavalcanti.
"Hey, friend!
where are we going then?"
he said, sticking his head through the opening.

He obeyed, not without anxiety; and as this anxiety grew minute by minute, after a few moments his mind, instead of the emptiness we noted when he set out, which had led to his sleep, his mind, let us say, was filled with a multitude of thoughts more than capable of keeping a traveler awake, especially a traveler in Danglars' situation.

sentences: Barbicane and his colleagues were staring intently at the intruder who boldly threw himself into the discussion.
None of them knew him, and the president, feeling uneasy about the outcome of such a straightforward conversation, looked at his new friend with some apprehension.
The assembly was attentive and seriously worried, as this debate had resulted in drawing their attention to the dangers or even the real impossibilities of the expedition.
--Oppose, sir, replied Michel Ardan with perfect gallantry, oppose as much as you like!
--You know, said the stranger, that when light rays pass through a medium like air, they are deflected from a straight line, or in other words, they undergo refraction.
Well!
when stars are obscured by the Moon, their rays, grazing the edges of the disc, have never experienced the slightest deflection nor given the faintest hint of refraction.
From this, it follows that the Moon is not surrounded by an atmosphere.
They looked at the Frenchman, for once the observation was accepted, the consequences were rigorous.

"Indeed, replied Michel Ardan, that is your best argument, if not the only one, and a scholar might be at a loss to respond; I will only tell you that this argument does not have absolute value, because it assumes the angular diameter of the Moon is perfectly determined, which it is not.
But let's move on, and tell me, my dear sir, if you accept the existence of volcanoes on the surface of the Moon.
--Let me believe, however, and without exceeding the bounds of logic, that these volcanoes were active for a certain period!
This is certain, but since they could provide the necessary oxygen for combustion themselves, the fact of their eruption does not prove the existence of a lunar atmosphere at all.
Let's move on then, replied Michel Ardan, and set aside this kind of argument to focus on direct observations.
But I warn you that I am going to name names.
No doubt; but without explaining the origin of these bright spots, Herschell himself did not conclude from their appearance that a lunar atmosphere was necessary.
Well said, said Michel Ardan, complimenting his opponent; I see that you are very knowledgeable in selenography.
